answer: Per DOC1, the crisis began with the U.S. housing downturn: housing prices, which had doubled since 2000, started declining in 2007. Many mortgage loans had been poor quality, and borrowers defaulted. Banks had bundled the mortgages into complex securities that were nearly impossible to value, so banks stopped lending to each other. This turned a housing decline into a financial crisis. Lehman Brothers went bankrupt on September 15, 2008, and the financial crisis became a major economic crisis and then a world recession.

Economists care mainly because of unemployment's direct effect on the welfare of the unemployed. It is often tied to financial and psychological suffering. When unemployment rises, it also becomes more painful. Many more people are unemployed, and many for a long time: mean duration was 9 weeks on average in 2000-2007 but 33 weeks in 2010. The U.S. rate rose from 4.6% in 2007 to 9.6% in 2010. Okun's law says weak growth raises unemployment, with a slope of -0.4. The text says there are two reasons, but the second reason is not on the pages provided.

Economists use real GDP instead of nominal GDP. Nominal GDP is quantities times current prices, so it reflects both quantity and price changes. Real GDP values output at common prices, so changes in it reflect quantities only. In the car example, real GDP at 2005 prices rises from $240,000 (2004) to $288,000 (2005), a 20% increase, and to $312,000 (2006), an 8% increase. In practice the U.S. uses chained (2005) dollars, with relative-price weights that change over time. Real GDP in 2010 was about 4.7 times its 1960 level, versus a 28-fold rise in nominal GDP. The GDP deflator (nominal GDP / real GDP) captures prices, so nominal growth = inflation + real growth. Growth is (Yt - Yt-1)/Yt-1.

The 2009 recession hit the world economy hard. World output fell 2.3% in 2009 (after +1.5% in 2008 and a 3.2% average in 2000-2007). Advanced economies shrank 3.7%, the lowest annual growth since the Great Depression. Emerging and developing economies still grew 2.8%, but that was nearly 4 points below their 6.5% 2000-2007 average. The crisis spread through trade and finance, and stock prices lost half or more of their value by the end of 2008.

U.S. unemployment jumped after the crisis, then fell. Rates were 4.6% (2007), 5.8% (2008), 9.3% (2009) and 9.6% in 2010, the peak. Sources conflict on 2010: DOC3 (medium trust) gives 9.8%, while DOC1 (high trust) gives 9.6%. I prefer 9.6%. DOC1 forecast 9.1% for 2011 and 9.0% for 2012. DOC2 outturns replace those forecasts: 8.9% in 2011, 8.1% in 2012, and 7.4% in 2013. That fall was faster than forecast.

Before the crisis, China's output growth averaged 9.8% a year in 1980–1999 and 10.5% in 2000–2007. During the crisis years it was 9.6% in 2008, 9.2% in 2009 and 10.3% in 2010 (DOC1 Table 1-4). The text says growth barely decreased, because a major fiscal expansion, especially public investment, offset weaker exports.

Not just the U.S. Document 1 says stock prices collapsed in the U.S., the Euro area and emerging economies. By the end of 2008 they had lost half or more of their value from their previous peak. Despite the crisis originating in the U.S., European and emerging-market stock prices fell as much as U.S. prices. It spread through trade (falling U.S. imports cut other countries' exports) and finance (U.S. banks repatriated funds). The result was a world recession: advanced-economy growth was -3.7% in 2009.

Not always; the link holds only on average. DOC1's Okun's law scatterplot has a slope of about -0.4, so each extra 1% of growth lowers the unemployment rate by roughly 0.4 points. About 3% growth is needed just to keep unemployment constant, because the labor force and output per worker both grow. Growth below that, even if positive, tends to raise unemployment. Growth is therefore only 'fast' enough when it exceeds roughly 3%. The relation is an average fit, not an iron rule. DOC2 outturns show that in 2012 U.S. growth of 2.3% (below 3%) came with unemployment falling from 8.9% to 8.1%, and unemployment fell more than the forecast implied.

No. DOC1 says the CPI and the GDP deflator move together most of the time: in most years the two inflation rates differ by less than 1%. There are clear exceptions, notably 1979 and 1980, when CPI inflation was significantly larger than GDP-deflator inflation. The cause: the GDP deflator prices goods produced in the U.S., while the CPI prices goods consumed, including imports. The price of oil doubled and the U.S. is a major oil importer, so the CPI rose faster. DOC3 (medium trust) also notes that the two measures can diverge, as in 2009.

Before the crisis Euro-area unemployment was already high: 9.6% (1980–99 average) and 8.5% (2000–07 average). DOC1 gives competing explanations. Some blame ECB policy for keeping interest rates too high. Others blame labor market institutions: costly layoffs deter hiring and generous unemployment insurance weakens job search. Skeptics note that the Netherlands and Denmark had rates under 4%, so implementation may matter more than the degree of protection. After the crisis: 9.5% (2009) and 10.1% (2010). DOC1's 2011 and 2012 forecasts of 9.9% are replaced by outturns of 10.2% (2011), 11.4% (2012) and 12.0% (2013), as output fell 0.7% in 2012 and 0.4% in 2013.

Document 1 says China's growth held up mainly because a major fiscal expansion by the government, especially a big rise in public investment, almost fully offset the fall in demand from slower exports. Demand and output kept growing. Output growth was 9.6% in 2008, 9.2% in 2009 and 10.3% in 2010, and unemployment barely rose (4.2%, 4.3%, 4.1%). The underlying sources of high growth are a very high investment rate (over 40% of output, against 17% in the U.S.) and rapid technological progress, helped by foreign firms and joint ventures.

Per DOC1, banks had bundled mortgages into new securities, repackaged them again and sold them to other banks and investors. Many banks held these securities, whose value was nearly impossible to assess. This complexity and opacity turned the housing price decline (with poor-quality loans and defaults) into a major financial crisis. Banks, unsure of each other's assets, became reluctant to lend to one another. After Lehman Brothers went bankrupt on September 15, 2008, links between banks were so opaque that many others seemed at risk, and the whole financial system looked as if it might collapse.

Document 1 says that falling housing prices, together with collapsing stock prices, made people sharply cut their consumption. Consumers who saw their housing and financial wealth fall kept cutting consumption, and housing prices were still declining in 2011. Lower housing prices were also expected to lower housing construction and consumer spending. Firms cut investment and few new homes were built. Demand and output fell, and U.S. output growth turned negative in Q3 2008 and stayed negative in 2009. No numeric estimate of the consumption response is given.

A recession is a decrease in output: a period of negative GDP growth. Periods of positive GDP growth are expansions. Economists often date recessions quarter by quarter rather than year by year. That is why people speak of a "recession of 2001" even though annual growth was positive that year. The NBER dates recessions: March to November 2001, and December 2007 to June 2009. The most recent recession was the most severe from 1960 to 2010, with zero U.S. growth in 2008 and a large negative rate in 2009.

Emerging and developing economies grew faster before the crisis. Over 2000–2007 their average output growth was 6.5% per year, versus 2.6% for advanced economies (world average 3.2%), a gap of 3.9 percentage points.

Lehman Brothers went bankrupt on September 15, 2008, according to Document 1. Its failure had dramatic effects: because its links to other banks were opaque, many other banks seemed at risk, and for a few weeks the whole financial system looked as if it might collapse.
